method: Each finding is computed by code from Fire Test Atlas rows; its claim is generated from the computed numbers, and it lists the rows used, the rows left out and why, what else differs between the tests, and what it does not establish. No language model writes or edits a finding.

findings.title: Less oxygen, and the flame goes out with more fuel left
findings.claim: In 9 of 10 groups of FLEX droplet burns (same fuel, added gas and pressure), flames that went out did so earlier, with more of the droplet unburned, the lower the oxygen (rank correlation -0.94 to 0, 154 runs). For methanol in nitrogen at about 1 atm, the flame went out at a median 0.73 of the starting droplet diameter at 12% O₂, against 0.41 at 30%.

excluded.reason: ended another way (disruption or burned away), so there is no extinction diameter
extinction or starting diameter, or oxygen, not recorded
pressure outside the 0.7 atm and 1 atm bands (about 3 atm, or written as 0)
group too small to measure a trend (fewer than 6 runs or 3 oxygen levels)

findings.method: 1. Take FLEX runs whose "Test end" is Extinction and that record both the starting droplet diameter and the visible flame extinction diameter. 2. Divide extinction diameter by starting diameter: 1 means the flame went out at once, near 0 that almost all the fuel burned. 3. Group runs by fuel, added gas (none, CO₂ or helium, from NASA's composition columns) and pressure band (0.7 atm: 9–12 psia; 1 atm: 12–16 psia). 4. In each group with at least 6 runs over 3 oxygen levels, compute Spearman's rank correlation between oxygen and the ratio. A negative value means less oxygen, more fuel left.

uncertainty.text: In 8 of 10 groups the 95% bootstrap interval of the rank correlation lies wholly below zero; in 2 it includes zero, so those groups alone do not show a direction. For methanol in nitrogen at about 1 atm the correlation is -0.68 (95% interval -0.83 to -0.43).
uncertainty.method: Percentile bootstrap: each group's runs resampled with replacement 2000 times (seeded, so the interval is the same on every rebuild), Spearman's correlation recomputed each time, and the middle 95% kept. Each run is treated as independent; runs made in the same session share hardware and conditions and may not be, which would make the interval too narrow. Session grouping has not been assessed.

confounders: Starting droplet size varies between runs (about 1.5 to 5 mm), and large droplets can go out from radiative heat loss at any oxygen level.
Where CO₂ or helium was added, its share changes with the oxygen level, so oxygen and added gas are not varied independently.
Runs that ended in disruption or burned away are left out, which removes the burns that lasted longest.
Each oxygen level has only one to a few runs in most groups.
findings.notClaimed: Liquid fuel droplets, not cabin solids. This shows a direction within FLEX's own runs; it is not an oxygen limit, a flammability prediction or a fire-safety rating.

findings.title: FLEX already burned fuel near Moon-base air
findings.claim: FLEX burned 17 fuel droplets at 30 and 34% O₂ and 10.33–10.5 psia, close to the challenge's exploration atmosphere (30% O₂ or more at 10.2 psi or less). None of these 17 flames went out before the droplet burned away or broke apart, against 14 of 29 in air at 1 atm.

excluded.reason: other oxygen levels, pressures or added gases

findings.method: 1. Take FLEX runs with no CO₂ or helium added. 2. High-oxygen set: oxygen of 30% or more in the 0.7 atm band (9–12 psia). Reference set: 21% oxygen in the 1 atm band (12–16 psia). 3. Count how each burn ended, from NASA's "Test end" column: Extinction (the flame went out), Disruption (the droplet broke apart) or Completion (it burned away).

uncertainty.text: Share of flames that went out: 0% of 17 near exploration air (95% interval 0–18%) against 48% of 29 in air (31–66%). With only 17 high-oxygen runs the first interval is wide.
uncertainty.method: Wilson score 95% interval for each proportion. Each run is treated as independent; runs made in the same session share hardware and conditions and may not be, which would make the interval too narrow. Session grouping has not been assessed.

confounders: The high-oxygen runs are at about 10.4 psia, slightly above the challenge's 10.2 psi, so their oxygen partial pressure is higher than the exploration atmosphere's.
The reference runs differ in pressure as well as oxygen.
Disruption (the droplet breaking apart) ends a burn before the fuel is used up; it is not the flame going out.
findings.notClaimed: These are liquid fuel droplets (methanol and n-heptane), not cabin materials, and they burned in microgravity, not lunar gravity. They are analogue evidence for exploration atmospheres, not a prediction for solids.

findings.title: Earth's test burned further than orbit, sample for sample
findings.claim: In 5 of 8 Saffire-II samples the 1-g ground test burned further than the same material did in orbit, 3 burned the same, and none burned further in orbit. 3 of the 4 silicone samples spread a flame on the ground but not in orbit (about 21.5–22.1% O₂, 20 cm/s air flow in orbit).

excluded.reason: composite PMMA + Nomex sample: NASA reports the two materials differently in the orbit and ground columns

findings.method: 1. For each Saffire-II sample, read NASA's µ-g burn length (orbit) and 1-g burn length (ground). 2. Put each on the same three-step scale: no spread (about 0), partial burn (a length in cm, short of the sample), whole sample ("Complete", or a µ-g length equal to the 29 cm sample). 3. Compare the two for the same sample.

uncertainty.text: If ground and orbit were equally likely to burn further, a split of 5 to 0 (ties left out) would happen by chance with probability 0.063 (two-sided sign test). That could be chance; these are only 8 samples of mostly different materials.
uncertainty.method: Exact two-sided sign test on the samples that differ; samples that burned the same on the ground and in orbit are left out. Each sample is treated as an independent pair.

confounders: The table does not say how the 1-g tests were set up (orientation, flow), so the ground flame may have been driven by buoyant flow rather than the 20 cm/s forced flow used in orbit.
One sample per material and thickness, at one oxygen level (about 22%).
Two samples have no material named in NASA's table; they are compared as pairs but not named.
findings.notClaimed: Eight samples at about 22% O₂ and 20 cm/s. This does not show that Earth tests are conservative in general: other NASA work suggests some materials burn more readily in low gravity under other flows and oxygen levels.

findings.title: Thick plastic fouled the air far more than fabric
findings.claim: In BASS-II's glovebox, a burn of thick PMMA (acrylic) slab raised carbon monoxide by a median 335 ppm (19 burns), about 17 times the 20 ppm of SIBAL fabric (25 burns). 4 more burns pushed CO off the sensor's scale, all of them PMMA.

excluded.reason: final O₂ implausible (a likely transcription slip), so the row's gas readings are not trusted
CO not recorded before or after the burn

findings.method: 1. Take every BASS-II burn. 2. Subtract NASA's "Initial CO (ppm)" from "Final CO (ppm)", and initial from final CO₂ (% by volume). 3. Group burns by material and form from the atlas material dictionary (PMMA slab, rod or film; SIBAL; Nomex; wax). 4. Report the median change per group. Readings NASA marks as off the scale (">500", "OR", "over") are counted separately, never given a number.

uncertainty.text: 95% bootstrap intervals: PMMA slab median 219 to 428 ppm, SIBAL fabric median 11 to 30 ppm, ratio 10 to 31 times. The 4 burns that pushed CO off the sensor's scale (all PMMA) are left out of the medians; counting them could only raise PMMA's figures.
uncertainty.method: Percentile bootstrap: each group's burns resampled with replacement 2000 times (seeded), medians and their ratio recomputed, middle 95% kept. Each burn is treated as independent; burns made in the same session share hardware and conditions and may not be, which would make the interval too narrow. Session grouping has not been assessed.

confounders: Burns differ in length, sample size, airflow and starting oxygen; the change is per burn, not per gram of fuel.
All burns share one glovebox volume, but the glovebox air was not always refreshed between burns, so starting levels differ.
NASA's headers call the O₂ readings calibrated but say nothing about the CO and CO₂ sensors.
Many PMMA rods and some films do not name their material; EMBER infers PMMA for them from the BASS-II record (marked in the table).
findings.notClaimed: A glovebox, not a cabin, and not a toxicity rating. It shows which BASS-II samples changed the glovebox air most, not how dangerous a cabin fire would be.

findings.title: Cool flames appeared in one narrow corner
findings.claim: 7 of 179 CFI-G normal-flame runs produced a cool flame, all with n-Butane (30% in nitrogen) at 2.03 bar and 38.9–39.9% O₂: 7 of the 17 runs at that fuel and pressure, and none of the other 162.
findings.method: 1. Take every CFI-G normal-flame run (fuel from the burner into an O₂/N₂ atmosphere). 2. A run has a cool flame when NASA's "Cool flame?" column starts with "yes". 3. Group runs by fuel and pressure (NASA's "approx p (bar)") and count cool flames in each.

uncertainty.text: At that fuel and pressure, cool flames appeared in 7 of 17 runs (95% interval 22–64%). None in the other 162 runs still allows a true rate of up to about 2% at those settings.
uncertainty.method: Wilson score 95% intervals; the upper bound for zero events is the Wilson upper limit. Each run is treated as independent; runs made in the same session share hardware and conditions and may not be, which would make the interval too narrow. Session grouping has not been assessed.

confounders: CFI-G set out to find cool flames, so the runs near these conditions were chosen where cool flames were expected; other settings were not searched as finely.
Oxygen fell during each run (NASA gives before and after values); the before value is used.
findings.notClaimed: Gas-fuel burner flames in microgravity. This maps where CFI-G saw cool flames; it does not say cool flames cannot happen elsewhere, or that they are a cabin hazard.

findings.title: Almost no solid has burned in exploration air
findings.claim: Of 402 solid-material tests, 145 record the oxygen level and only 5 the pressure. Solid tests in NASA's PSI tables stop at 22.2% O₂; 4 samples from the Saffire IV–VI paper go higher, and 2 of them reach the challenge's exploration atmosphere (SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric at 31% and 7.85 psia; PMMA at 30.3% and 7.92 psia). Both burned.

numbers.inZoneList: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric at 31% and 7.85 psia; PMMA at 30.3% and 7.92 psia

excluded.reason: solid tests that do not record oxygen (e.g. BASS, Saffire-III, SAME)

findings.method: 1. Take every test in the atlas whose fuel is a solid. 2. Use its oxygen (the top of the range where NASA lists a range) and pressure where recorded. 3. Find the highest oxygen in the PSI tables, then the tests above it, and those at 30% O₂ or more and 10.2 psi or less.

uncertainty.text: This is a count of the tests that exist in these sources, not an estimate from a sample, so it has no sampling interval. It is only as complete as the sources: a test outside PSI and the Saffire IV–VI paper is not counted.
uncertainty.method: No statistical test: every solid test in the atlas is counted.

confounders: PSI solid tests at 21–22% O₂ ran in the ISS cabin or glovebox at about 1 atm, but the tables do not record pressure, so they cannot be placed on both axes.
The Saffire IV–VI values come from a NASA conference paper (NTRS 20240002981), not from PSI.
findings.notClaimed: Counts what has been tested, from these sources. It does not say how solids would burn in exploration air, or that tests outside these sources do not exist.

findings.title: Almost every small burn raised carbon monoxide
findings.claim: Carbon monoxide rose in 117 of 118 BASS-II glovebox burns with readings before and after (99%). The median burn added 45 ppm, one in ten added 413 ppm or more, and the largest 575 ppm; 41 burns (35%) added 100 ppm or more, and 4 more pushed CO off the sensor's scale.

excluded.reason: final O₂ implausible (a likely transcription slip), so the row's gas readings are not trusted
CO not recorded before or after the burn

findings.method: 1. Take every BASS-II burn. 2. Subtract NASA's "Initial CO (ppm)" from "Final CO (ppm)". 3. Report how many burns rose, the median, the 90th percentile and the largest rise, and how many reached 100 ppm. Readings NASA marks as off the scale are counted separately, never given a number.

uncertainty.text: Share of burns where CO rose: 95% interval 95–100%. Median rise: 95% bootstrap interval 31 to 66 ppm. Off-scale burns are left out of the median, so it is if anything an underestimate.
uncertainty.method: Wilson score interval for the share; percentile bootstrap (2000 seeded resamples) for the median. Each burn is treated as independent; burns made in the same session share hardware and conditions and may not be, which would make the interval too narrow. Session grouping has not been assessed.

confounders: The glovebox air was not always refreshed between burns: starting CO ranged up to 660 ppm (median 7 ppm), so some burns ran in air that already held CO.
Burns differ in material, sample size, length, airflow and oxygen (F4 splits them by material).
A glovebox holds far less air than a cabin, so the same fire would raise cabin CO much less; and NASA's headers say nothing about calibrating the CO sensor.
findings.notClaimed: Not a detector setting, an alarm threshold or a toxicity rating, and it does not compare CO with smoke detection. It shows that these small burns produced CO a gas sensor could register, in a glovebox.

findings.title: Spacecraft smoke particles grew as the smoke aged
findings.claim: In 46 of 48 SAME and SAME-R runs measured both fresh and after ageing, the smoke's mean particle diameter grew. The median run grew 1.5 times (SAME 1.33 times over 8 runs, SAME-R 1.59 times over 40). Across the runs, the median fresh diameter was 0.19 µm and the median aged diameter 0.27 µm; fresh smoke was measured a median 38 s after it was made and aged smoke 623 s.
findings.unit: runs, each measured fresh and aged

excluded.reason: the sheet holds no mean diameter for the fresh or the aged row (NASA wrote 0 or an error value)

findings.method: 1. Take NASA's SAME and SAME-R results workbook ("Reduced data sheet"). 2. Group its rows by run: sample type plus SAME test number, where a number ending in "a" is the aged measurement of that run. 3. Keep runs with exactly one fresh and one aged row whose flight, material, inlet velocity and heater setting agree. 4. Use NASA's "M1/M0 (micro-m)--AMD" column, the mean particle diameter from the first two moments of the size distribution; a 0 or an error value means the sheet holds no diameter for that row, and the run is left out. 5. Divide aged by fresh diameter for each run, then take the median of those ratios. The two median diameters and the two median times are each taken across runs and do not describe one run.

uncertainty.text: Share of runs that grew: 95% interval 86–99%. Median growth: 95% bootstrap interval 1.28 to 1.64 times.
uncertainty.method: Wilson score interval for the share; percentile bootstrap (2000 seeded resamples) of whole runs for the median ratio. Both treat each run as independent; runs made on the same day or from the same sample carousel may not be, which would make the intervals too narrow.

confounders: 40 of the 48 runs are SAME-R and 8 SAME; the two flights differ in materials and heater settings.
Ageing time, heater temperature and flow differ between runs; the ratio does not separate them.
Some particles can deposit on chamber walls while the smoke ages, which also changes the measured mean size.
This is the count-weighted mean diameter. NASA's mass-based diameter is a different measure and is not used here.
findings.notClaimed: Smoke from heated (not flaming) materials in an experiment chamber, not a cabin fire. It does not set a detector design, give a growth rate, or say how fast cabin smoke ages.
